findings.body: The code canonicalizes both root and candidate paths, but then strips the root prefix from the candidate. If the candidate path resolves to a file outside the root directory (e.g., via symlinks or relative components), strip_prefix will fail and return PermissionDenied. However, if strip_prefix succeeds (e.g., when the resolved candidate is exactly under root), the code proceeds to open the file. The issue is that canonicalize() resolves symlinks, but if the original name contains '..' components that resolve to a path outside root after canonicalization, the check may not prevent access to files outside the intended directory.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker could provide a name like '../../../etc/passwd' that, when joined with root and canonicalized, resolves to a sensitive system file outside the intended root directory. If strip_prefix does not catch this (e.g., due to symlink resolution quirks or platform differences), the file could be opened, leading to unauthorized file access.
findings.title: Path traversal vulnerability in file path resolution

findings.body: The change replaces ProcessBuilder with Runtime.exec using /bin/sh -c, which passes the user input through a shell. findings.body: The change replaces exec.Command("report", "--user", user) with exec.Command("sh", "-c", "report --user "+user), which invokes a shell and concatenates the user string directly into the command. This violates the spec requirement that 'Report commands shall pass user names as arguments without a shell' and introduces a shell injection vulnerability.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious user string containing shell metacharacters (e.g., 'alice; rm -rf /') would be executed by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution instead of being passed safely as a single argument to the report command.
findings.title: Command execution now uses shell instead of direct arguments

findings.body: The change modifies return rows to return rows[1:], which drops the first row. This contradicts the spec requirement that 'Rendering shall preserve every row'.
findings.failure_scenario: When Render is called with rows containing data, the first row is silently dropped, causing data loss in the report output.
findings.title: Rendering no longer preserves every row as required

findings.body: The test function was renamed from TestRenderPreservesRows to TestRenderReturnsRows, but the new name does not accurately describe what the test checks (it only checks for nil, not that rows are returned).
findings.failure_scenario: Future maintainers may misinterpret the test's purpose and miss regressions where rows are incorrectly dropped or modified.
findings.title: Test name no longer reflects its purpose

findings.body: The test was renamed from TestRenderPreservesRows to TestRenderReturnsRows and its assertion changed to only check for nil, losing the original validation that all rows are preserved.
findings.failure_scenario: The test no longer catches cases where rows are dropped or modified, reducing confidence in the correctness of the Render function.

findings.body: The user input is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`, enabling command injection if the user string contains shell metacharacters like semicolons, pipes, or backticks.
findings.failure_scenario: When a malicious user provides input like 'alice; rm -rf /', the shell executes the injected command after the report command, potentially causing arbitrary code execution.
findings.title: Prevent OS command injection via user input

findings.body: The change replaces return rows with return rows.sublist(1), which drops the first row. This contradicts the spec requirement that 'Rendering shall preserve every row'.
findings.failure_scenario: When rendering a report, the first data row is silently dropped, causing incomplete reports to be generated.
findings.title: Report rendering no longer preserves every row

findings.body: The change replaces Process.run('report', ['--user', user]) with Process.run('sh', ['-c', command]), which passes the command through a shell. This contradicts the spec requirement that 'Report commands shall pass user names as arguments without a shell'.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious user name containing shell metacharacters (e.g., 'alice; rm -rf /') would be interpreted by the shell, enabling command injection attacks.
findings.title: Command execution now uses shell instead of direct arguments

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The test was changed from verifying the exact output ['first', 'second'] to only checking isNotNull, which no longer validates that all rows are preserved as required by the spec.
findings.failure_scenario: The test will pass even if rows are dropped or modified, failing to catch regressions in row preservation.
findings.title: Test no longer validates row preservation

findings.body: The actions/labeler@v6 action requires write permissions on pull requests to apply labels. While the diff adds 'pull-requests: write', it is critical to ensure this permission is scoped narrowly and that the action is configured to only label based on trusted file patterns to avoid unintended label assignment.
findings.failure_scenario: If the labeler action is misconfigured with overly broad file patterns or if an attacker can manipulate file paths in a PR, they could trigger label assignment that affects workflow logic or access control.
findings.title: Add explicit permissions for labeler action

findings.body: Switching from `pull_request` to `pull_request_target` changes the execution context to the base branch instead of the PR branch. This is often used to allow workflows to access secrets while still reacting to PR events, but it introduces risk if the workflow runs untrusted code from the PR branch (e.g., via actions or scripts checked into the PR). Without additional safeguards, malicious PRs could inject harmful logic that runs with elevated permissions.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR author could add a step or action in their PR that executes arbitrary code when this workflow runs, potentially exfiltrating repository secrets or modifying protected resources.
findings.title: Change from pull_request to pull_request_target may expose workflow to PR-based attacks

findings.body: The new permissions block grants read access to contents and write access to pull-requests, but there is no documentation explaining why these specific permissions are required or whether they align with the principle of least privilege.
findings.failure_scenario: If these permissions exceed what is needed for the labeler action, it could violate the principle of least privilege and increase the attack surface in case of workflow compromise.
findings.title: Add documentation for the new permissions block

ground_truth.clean_trap: pull_request_target is intentional for labeling; checkout stays on the trusted base revision and no secret is exposed to fork code.
ground_truth.name: github-actions-clean-context-v1
